shared.concept_anchor: Joint sitting presided by Speaker of Lok Sabha, not Chairman of Rajya Sabha

en.display_text:
A joint sitting of Parliament summoned by the President under Article 108 to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary bill is presided over by the ________.

(a) Vice President of India in his capacity as ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha
(b) Speaker of Lok Sabha, or the Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha in the Speaker's absence
(c) President of India who summons the joint sitting and retains presiding authority throughout
(d) Chairman of Rajya Sabha, since the upper House is the one whose position is being contested in the deadlock
en.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because the Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Vice President) is a senior constitutional functionary, and students assume a joint function of both Houses would be presided by the head of the upper house.
elimination_logic: Recall: Article 118(4) read with parliamentary practice — the Speaker of Lok Sabha presides at joint sittings.
Eliminate option (a): the Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha but has no presiding role at joint sittings.
Eliminate option (c): the President of India does not preside over legislative proceedings.
Eliminate option (d): the Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Vice President) does not preside at joint sittings — Speaker of Lok Sabha does.
Confirm option (b): the Speaker of Lok Sabha presides — or the Deputy Speaker in the Speaker's absence.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces 'Speaker of Lok Sabha' with 'Chairman of Rajya Sabha.' The intuitive reasoning that causes the error is: since Rajya Sabha is involved in the joint sitting, its presiding officer must co-chair or chair. This logic, while intuitive, is constitutionally incorrect. The Speaker of Lok Sabha presides — a rule that also symbolically reflects Lok Sabha's numerical dominance in such a setting.
en.final_explanation:
A joint sitting of Parliament under Article 108, when summoned by the President to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary bill, is presided over by a specific constitutional functionary.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha. While this is a senior constitutional office, the Vice President/Chairman has no presiding role at joint sittings.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting. In the absence of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha presides. The Chairman of Rajya Sabha has no presiding role.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The President summons the joint sitting but does not preside over it — summoning and presiding are two different constitutional functions.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Vice President) does not preside at joint sittings. This is the most common misconception.

Value Addition:
• The Speaker's presiding role at joint sittings reinforces Lok Sabha's pre-eminence in the legislative process for ordinary bills.
• The Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha (not of Rajya Sabha) is the second in line to preside.
• Only three joint sittings have occurred in India's history — in 1961, 1978, and 2002.

hi.display_text:
अनुच्छेद 108 के तहत राष्ट्रपति द्वारा आम विधेयक पर गतिरोध को सुलझाने के लिए बुलाई गई संसद की संयुक्त बैठक की अध्यक्षता ________ द्वारा की जाती है।

(a) भारत के उपराष्ट्रपति के रूप में, जो पदेन राज्यसभा के अध्यक्ष हैं
(b) लोकसभा के अध्यक्ष द्वारा, या अध्यक्ष के अनुपस्थित होने पर लोकसभा के उपाध्यक्ष द्वारा
(c) भारत के राष्ट्रपति द्वारा, जो संयुक्त बैठक बुलाते हैं और पूरी बैठक में अध्यक्षता बनाए रखते हैं
(d) राज्यसभा के अध्यक्ष द्वारा, क्योंकि उच्च सदन वह है जिसका पद गतिरोध में विवादित है
hi.strong_distractor: d — विकल्प (d) भ्रामक है क्योंकि राज्यसभा के अध्यक्ष (उपराष्ट्रपति) एक वरिष्ठ संवैधानिक पदाधिकारी हैं, और छात्र मान लेते हैं कि दोनों सदनों के संयुक्त कार्य का संचालन उच्च सदन के प्रमुख द्वारा किया जाएगा।
elimination_logic: स्मरण करें: अनुच्छेद 118(4) और संसदीय प्रथा के अनुसार — संयुक्त बैठकों की अध्यक्षता लोकसभा के अध्यक्ष करते हैं।
विकल्प (a) को हटाएं: उपराष्ट्रपति राज्यसभा के पदेन अध्यक्ष हैं लेकिन संयुक्त बैठकों में उनकी कोई अध्यक्षता भूमिका नहीं होती।
विकल्प (c) को हटाएं: भारत के राष्ट्रपति विधायी कार्यवाही की अध्यक्षता नहीं करते।
विकल्प (d) को हटाएं: राज्यसभा के अध्यक्ष (उपराष्ट्रपति) संयुक्त बैठकों की अध्यक्षता नहीं करते — यह कार्य लोकसभा के अध्यक्ष का होता है।
विकल्प (b) की पुष्टि करें: संयुक्त बैठक की अध्यक्षता लोकसभा के अध्यक्ष करते हैं — या अध्यक्ष के अनुपस्थित होने पर उपाध्यक्ष करते हैं।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: यह entity-swap जाल 'लोकसभा के अध्यक्ष' को 'राज्यसभा के अध्यक्ष' से बदल देता है। त्रुटि का सहज तर्क यह है कि चूंकि राज्यसभा संयुक्त बैठक में शामिल है, इसलिए उसकी अध्यक्षता करने वाले अधिकारी को सह-अध्यक्ष या अध्यक्ष होना चाहिए। यह तर्क सहज है, लेकिन संवैधानिक रूप से गलत है। संयुक्त बैठक की अध्यक्षता लोकसभा के अध्यक्ष करते हैं — जो इस बात का प्रतीकात्मक रूप से भी संकेत है कि ऐसी स्थिति में लोकसभा की संख्या में श्रेष्ठता होती है।
hi.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 108 के तहत राष्ट्रपति द्वारा आम विधेयक पर गतिरोध को सुलझाने के लिए बुलाई गई संसद की संयुक्त बैठक की अध्यक्षता एक विशिष्ट संवैधानिक पदाधिकारी द्वारा की जाती है।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: उपराष्ट्रपति राज्यसभा के पदेन अध्यक्ष हैं। यह एक वरिष्ठ संवैधानिक पद है, लेकिन उपराष्ट्रपति/अध्यक्ष की संयुक्त बैठकों में कोई अध्यक्षता भूमिका नहीं होती।
• विकल्प (b) — सही: संयुक्त बैठक की अध्यक्षता लोकसभा के अध्यक्ष करते हैं। अध्यक्ष के अनुपस्थित होने पर लोकसभा के उपाध्यक्ष अध्यक्षता करते हैं। राज्यसभा के अध्यक्ष की कोई अध्यक्षता भूमिका नहीं होती।
• विकल्प (c) — गलत: राष्ट्रपति संयुक्त बैठक बुलाते हैं लेकिन उसकी अध्यक्षता नहीं करते — बुलाने और अध्यक्षता करना दो अलग संवैधानिक कार्य हैं।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: राज्यसभा के अध्यक्ष (उपराष्ट्रपति) संयुक्त बैठकों की अध्यक्षता नहीं करते। यह सबसे सामान्य भ्रांति है।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• संयुक्त बैठकों में अध्यक्ष की भूमिका लोकसभा की विधायी प्रक्रिया में प्रधानता को पुष्ट करती है।
• लोकसभा के उपाध्यक्ष (राज्यसभा के नहीं) अध्यक्ष के बाद दूसरे नंबर पर होते हैं।
• भारत के इतिहास में केवल तीन संयुक्त बैठकें हुई हैं — 1961, 1978, और 2002।

Pocket Veto vs. Absolute Veto vs. Suspensive Veto

shared.concept_anchor: Article 143 advisory opinion is non-binding; cannot substitute Article 111

en.display_text:
Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional position when Parliament re-passes an ordinary bill after the President has returned it for reconsideration under Article 111?

(a) The President must give assent to the re-passed bill — there is no power to return it again or to refer its constitutionality to the Supreme Court under Article 143 as a substitute for assent
(b) The President may refer the re-passed bill to the Supreme Court under Article 143 for a binding opinion on its constitutionality before deciding whether to give assent
(c) The President retains the power to withhold assent permanently on re-passed bills, as the return and re-passage constitute an absolute veto override mechanism
(d) If Parliament re-passes the bill with modifications suggested by the President, assent is mandatory; but if re-passed without the suggested modifications, the President may invoke the pocket veto indefinitely
en.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly states that Article 143 exists as an advisory reference mechanism, but falsely implies it can be used to delay assent to a pending bill, which is a partial truth that obscures the non-binding nature.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): while Article 143 exists, it cannot be used as a constitutionality check on a specific pending bill as a substitute for Article 111 action — and the opinion is non-binding in any event.
Eliminate option (c): the President's power to return a bill under Article 111 is a suspensive veto, not an absolute one — Parliament can override by re-passing.
Eliminate option (d): the President cannot permanently keep a bill pending after Parliament re-passes it — the pocket veto operates only before re-passage, and after re-passage assent is mandatory.

Confirm option (a): after Parliament re-passes a returned bill under Article 111 (with or without amendments), the President must give assent — there is no absolute veto for ordinary bills at that stage.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is a partial-truth trap: it correctly identifies Article 143 as an advisory reference mechanism but implies it can be invoked to avoid or delay Presidential assent under Article 111. Article 143 opinions are non-binding — they cannot validate or invalidate a bill. Using Article 143 as a delaying tactic for assent would itself be unconstitutional. A partially prepared student who knows Article 143 exists as a Presidential reference tool will be tempted by option (b).
en.final_explanation:
The interaction between Presidential assent (Article 111) and advisory opinions (Article 143) is a nuanced constitutional question.

• Option (a) — Correct: If Parliament re-passes an ordinary bill after the President returns it for reconsideration (under the suspensive veto), the President must give assent. There is no power to refuse a second time — this is the constitutional override of the suspensive veto. Parliament's re-passage — whether with the President's suggested changes or without — is final.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 143 empowers the President to refer questions of law or public importance to the Supreme Court. It cannot be used to delay or avoid assent by seeking a constitutionality opinion on a pending bill. The Supreme Court's opinion under Article 143 is advisory and non-binding — it does not validate or invalidate legislation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The President's power under Article 111 to return a bill is a suspensive veto — Parliament can override. It is not an absolute veto.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: After Parliament re-passes a returned bill, the President must give assent. The pocket veto (indefinite inaction) applies only before any Presidential action, not after re-passage.

Value Addition:
• The Kerala Education Bill (1958) reference under Article 143 occurred before Presidential assent — a rare legitimate use of Article 143 concerning a bill.
• India's President cannot exercise judicial review over bills — that power belongs to courts after enactment.
• The constitutional design ensures no absolute Presidential veto over ordinary bills — Parliament ultimately prevails.

hi.display_text:
जब संसद राष्ट्रपति द्वारा अनुच्छेद 111 के तहत पुनर्विचार के लिए वापस किए गए सामान्य विधेयक को पुनः पारित करता है, तो निम्नलिखित में से कौन-सा संवैधानिक स्थिति को सही रूप से वर्णित करता है?

(a) राष्ट्रपति को पुनः पारित विधेयक को स्वीकृति देनी होगी — इसे फिर से वापस करने या अनुच्छेद 143 के तहत उसकी संवैधानिकता को सुप्रीम कोर्ट के समक्ष संदर्भित करने का अधिकार नहीं है
(b) राष्ट्रपति पुनः पारित विधेयक को अनुच्छेद 143 के तहत उसकी संवैधानिकता पर बाध्यकारी राय के लिए सुप्रीम कोर्ट के समक्ष भेज सकते हैं, फिर स्वीकृति देने का निर्णय ले सकते हैं
(c) राष्ट्रपति के पास पुनः पारित विधेयकों पर स्थायी रूप से स्वीकृति रोकने का अधिकार है, क्योंकि वापस करना और पुनः पारित करना पूर्ण वीटो ओवरराइड तंत्र है

• केरल शिक्षा विधेयक (1958) का अनुच्छेद 143 के तहत संदर्भ राष्ट्रपति की स्वीकृति से पहले हुआ था — विधेयक से संबंधित अनुच्छेद 143 का एक दुर्लभ वैध उपयोग।
• भारत के राष्ट्रपति विधेयकों पर न्यायिक समीक्षा का प्रयोग नहीं कर सकते — वह अधिकार अधिनियम के बाद न्यायालयों का है।

en.display_text:
With reference to the fate of ordinary bills upon dissolution of Lok Sabha and the role of Presidential notification, consider the following statements:

1. If a bill that was pending in Lok Sabha lapses due to dissolution of Lok Sabha, the President can notify that the bill shall not be treated as lapsed — enabling a joint sitting even after a fresh Lok Sabha is constituted.
2. A bill that has been passed by Rajya Sabha but has not been taken up by Lok Sabha is revived automatically when a new Lok Sabha is constituted after dissolution.
3. The joint sitting convened after Presidential notification to prevent lapsing of a bill can include members of the newly elected Lok Sabha along with continuing Rajya Sabha members.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
(a) 1 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 1 and 3 only

statement_analysis.statement: If a bill that was pending in Lok Sabha lapses due to dissolution of Lok Sabha, the President can notify that the bill shall not be treated as lapsed — enabling a joint sitting even after a fresh Lok Sabha is constituted.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution provides the President with the power to notify that a bill shall not be treated as having lapsed, allowing the possibility of a joint sitting even with the newly constituted Lok Sabha.

statement_analysis.statement: A bill that has been passed by Rajya Sabha but has not been taken up by Lok Sabha is revived automatically when a new Lok Sabha is constituted after dissolution.
statement_analysis.reason: A bill passed by Rajya Sabha but pending in Lok Sabha lapses on Lok Sabha dissolution. It does not automatically revive — it requires Presidential notification under the relevant provision of Article 108.

statement_analysis.statement: The joint sitting convened after Presidential notification to prevent lapsing of a bill can include members of the newly elected Lok Sabha along with continuing Rajya Sabha members.
statement_analysis.reason: The joint sitting after Presidential notification is not limited to the old Lok Sabha. Once a new Lok Sabha is constituted, its members participate in the joint sitting alongside continuing Rajya Sabha members.

en.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because Statement 2 sounds legally sound — students who know bills in Rajya Sabha don't lapse may incorrectly think 'Rajya Sabha origin' protects a bill pending in Lok Sabha.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 as correct — Presidential notification can preserve a lapsed bill for joint sitting, even with a newly constituted Lok Sabha.
Evaluate Statement 2 — a bill pending in Lok Sabha (even if Rajya Sabha-originated) lapses on dissolution; it does not automatically revive — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — the joint sitting post-notification includes newly elected Lok Sabha members.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (d).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a scope-extension trap that extends the 'Rajya Sabha bills don't lapse' principle beyond its actual scope. The rule that Rajya Sabha bills don't lapse on dissolution refers to bills pending exclusively in Rajya Sabha. Once such a bill has been passed by Rajya Sabha and transmitted to Lok Sabha, it is Lok Sabha's pending business and lapses on dissolution — regardless of where it originated.
en.final_explanation:
The interaction between dissolution of Lok Sabha, lapsing of bills, and Presidential notification for joint sitting involves layered rules that must be carefully distinguished.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The President has an extraordinary power to notify that a bill shall not be treated as having lapsed upon Lok Sabha dissolution. This enables a joint sitting to be held even after the newly elected Lok Sabha takes office — preserving legislative continuity for important bills.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: A bill passed by Rajya Sabha but pending in Lok Sabha lapses when Lok Sabha is dissolved — it does not matter that it originated in or was passed by Rajya Sabha. The lapsing rule is based on where the bill is currently pending, not where it originated. Automatic revival does not occur.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The joint sitting enabled by Presidential notification is a living legislative forum — it involves the newly constituted Lok Sabha members alongside the continuing Rajya Sabha members. It is not a historical fiction of the old Lok Sabha meeting again.

Value Addition:
• Presidential notification to prevent lapsing is an extraordinary power — rarely invoked in practice.
• After prorogation (not dissolution), pending bills do not lapse — prorogation merely suspends the session.
• The joint sitting is a legislative mechanism, not a constitutional court — it cannot adjudicate on the bill's validity.
